trial.title: Impact of Exercise Associated With Cognitive-behavioral Therapy in Smokers

endpoints.description: The primary outcome of this study is the smoking cessation rate, defined as the percentage of participants who remain abstinent from tobacco use during the follow-up period. To ensure the robustness of the results, abstinence will be verified by participants' self-reports and confirmed by biochemical measures performed by physicians, such as blood cotinine levels and/or exhaled carbon monoxide (CO) testing. The selection of this primary outcome is based on the clinical relevance of achieving smoking cessation, as it contributes to improved individual health and serves as a direct indicator of the effectiveness of the proposed combined intervention.

outcome.rationale: Three-arm design with active comparators and no placebo control makes 'success' definition ambiguous. Trial likely to show numerically higher abstinence in CBT+Exercise vs Health Guidelines (consistent with Abrantes 2014 trend), but small sample (n=66, ~22 per arm) limits power to detect statistically significant differences. No pharmacotherapy may limit absolute abstinence rates. Trial may demonstrate feasibility and acceptability but definitive efficacy conclusions unlikely given design constraints. Prediction confidence limited by lack of direct efficacy data and null results from larger exercise studies.

analysis_trace.content: NCT07186049: 'Impact of Exercise Associated With Cognitive-behavioral Therapy in Smokers' - A 3-arm parallel randomized trial testing CBT alone vs CBT+Exercise vs General Health Guidelines for smoking cessation in adult smokers. Status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING, expected completion April 2027, n=66.

Primary endpoint (primary-0): Smoking cessation rate at 12 weeks, defined as percentage abstinent verified by self-report and biochemical confirmation (cotinine and/or exhaled CO). This is a binary proportion outcome measured at a single post-treatment timepoint. Direction: higher is better (favors intervention).

Adult smokers (≥18 years) with active combustible cigarette smoking. Exclusions: unstable heart disease, severe orthopedic problems, cognitive disorders. Population represents typical treatment-seeking smokers without major medical contraindications to exercise.

CBT targets maladaptive thoughts and behaviors through coping skills and relapse prevention. Exercise adjunct is hypothesized to reduce withdrawal symptoms, cravings, and weight gain concerns. Evidence suggests exercise may improve mood and adherence but meta-analyses show mixed results for abstinence outcomes.

Key evidence retrieved: (1) Dunsiger et al. 2021 (PMC11619333): RCT of exercise+NRT vs control+NRT in women smokers found NO significant difference in cotinine-verified abstinence at 12 weeks or follow-up. Evidence role: direct_mechanism, numeric_use_allowed=false (different population/women only, with NRT). (2) Abrantes et al. 2014 (PMC4155424): Preliminary RCT of behavioral exercise intervention showed non-significant trend favoring exercise (40% vs 22.6% at EOT). Evidence role: indirect_direction, numeric_use_allowed=true with uncertainty (combined CBT+exercise, similar design). (3) Vinci 2020 (PMC7874528): Review confirming CBT efficacy for smoking cessation. Evidence role: mechanism_background.

No exact population/intervention match found. Abrantes 2014 closest: behavioral exercise intervention with telephone CBT, 12-week program, 61 smokers. Key differences: included NRT, different CBT delivery mode. Dunsiger 2021: supervised exercise, NRT provided, women only, null result for exercise effect. Current trial has no pharmacotherapy, smaller sample (n=66 vs n=105-164 in prior studies).

Based on Abrantes 2014 (exercise+CBT showed 40% vs 22.6% control at EOT, non-significant) and general CBT literature (20-35% abstinence), predict: Group 1 (CBT alone): 25-35%; Group 2 (CBT+Exercise): 28-40%; Group 3 (Health Guidelines): 15-25%. Wide uncertainty due to small sample, no direct efficacy data, and null results from larger exercise studies.
Behavioral interventions only, minimal safety concerns. Exercise component may carry low risk of musculoskeletal injury. No serious safety signals expected.

Primary risks to trial success: (1) Small sample size (n=66) limits statistical power to detect between-group differences; (2) No pharmacotherapy adjunct may reduce overall abstinence rates vs medication-assisted trials; (3) Exercise adherence may be poor (historically 50-70% in similar trials); (4) Three-arm design further reduces per-group power; (5) General Health Guidelines may be more active than pure control, potentially attenuating effect sizes.

Evidence chain: Abrantes 2014 provides directional support for exercise+CBT superiority (OR~2.0) but with wide CIs. Dunsiger 2021 suggests null effect when exercise is adjunct to NRT, but different population and intervention. Meta-analytic evidence (Ussher et al.) shows exercise does not significantly improve cessation when added to standard treatment. Therefore, predicted effect of exercise addition is modest (5-10 percentage point improvement) with low confidence. CBT alone expected to show meaningful abstinence (25-35%) based on established efficacy.

No direct results from this trial available (not yet recruiting). No identical intervention trials found. Limited evidence for CBT+Exercise without pharmacotherapy. Sample size smaller than prior positive studies. Geographic/cultural factors unknown (trial likely in Brazil based on 'Thesis' arm naming).
